top_cited_works.title: Separation Control Using Plasma Actuators: Dynamic Stall Vortex Control on Oscillating Airfoil
top_cited_works.abstract: A plasma actuator was used to control leading-edge flow separation and dynamic stall vortex on a periodically oscillated NACA 0015 airfoil. The effectiveness of the actuator was documented through phase-conditioned surface pressure measurements and smoke flow visualization records. The airfoil was driven in a periodic cycle corresponding to α = 15 deg+10deg sinwt. The results presented here are for a reduced frequency of k = ωc/2U ∞ = 0.08. Three cases of control with the plasma actuator were investigated: open-loop control with steady plasma actuation, open-loop control with unsteady plasma actuation, and closed-loop control with steady plasma actuation. For closed-loop control, the actuator was activated in selected portions of the oscillatory cycle based on angle-of-attack feedback. All of the cases investigated exhibited an increase in cycle-integrated lift with improvements in the lift-cycle hysteresis. In two cases, the pitch-moment stall angle was delayed and in one of these, the adverse negative moment peak was significantly reduced.

top_cited_works.title: Plasma Actuators for Cylinder Flow Control and Noise Reduction
top_cited_works.abstract: In this paper, the results of flow-control experiments using single dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuators to control flow separation and unsteady vortex shedding from a circular cylinder in crossflow are reported. This work is motivated by the need to reduce landing gear noise for commercial transport aircraft via an effective streamlining created by the actuators. The experiments are performed at Re D = 3.3 x 104. Using either steady or unsteady actuation, Karman shedding is totally eliminated, turbulence levels in the wake decrease significantly, and near-field sound pressure levels associated with shedding are reduced by 13.3 dB. In the case of unsteady plasma actuation, an actuation frequency of St D = 1 is found to be most effective. The unsteady actuation has the advantage that total suppression of shedding is achieved for a duty cycle of only 25%. However, because unsteady actuation is associated with an unsteady body force and produces a tone at the actuation frequency, steady actuation is more suitable for noise-control applications.

top_cited_works.title: Dielectric Barrier Discharge Plasma Actuators for Flow Control
top_cited_works.abstract: The term plasma actuator has now been a part of the fluid dynamics flow-control vernacular for more than a decade. A particular type of plasma actuator that has gained wide use is based on a single–dielectric barrier discharge (SDBD) mechanism that has desirable features for use in air at atmospheric pressures. For these actuators, the mechanism of flow control is through a generated body-force vector field that couples with the momentum in the external flow. The body force can be derived from first principles, and the effect of plasma actuators can be easily incorporated into flow solvers so that their placement and operation can be optimized. They have been used in a wide range of internal and external flow applications. Although initially considered useful only at low speeds, plasma actuators are effective in a number of applications at high subsonic, transonic, and supersonic Mach numbers, owing largely to more optimized actuator designs that were developed through better understanding and modeling of the actuator physics. recent_works.title: Adaptive Gaussian Process Control of Turbulent Transition via Dynamic Wavelength Plasma Roughness (DWPR) at Mach 6
recent_works.abstract: A dielectric barrier discharge actuator with dynamic wavelength capability was designed, manufactured, and tested for active control of stationary cross-flow transition on a 70-degree swept fin mounted to a 7-degree half-angle cone at Mach 5.85 in the Notre Dame STEM Mach 6 Ludwieg Tube. Baseline infrared measurements identified naturally dominant transition wavelengths near 28 mm, which motivated a subcritical forcing wavelength of 20 mm. Open-loop control experiments demonstrated that the subcritical forcing was most effective at a yaw angle of -0.5 degrees. The naturally dominant wavelength (unforced) was near 23.4 mm for a yaw angle of -0.5 degrees. Run-to-run closed-loop control was then performed to autonomously drive the surface heating on the fin toward a global minimum.

recent_works.title: Design and Characterization of the Notre Dame Mach 4 Reflected Shock Tunnel (M4ST)
Investigating the Use of a Gliding Arc for the Control of the Shock-Wave/Boundary Layer Interaction
recent_works.abstract: A glide arc style actuator was tested at the University of Notre Dame at Mach 3 to study its effect on the shock-wave/boundary layer interaction (SWBLI). Using a 14$^\circ$ shock generator, an impinging shock interaction was formed with a turbulent boundary layer at unit Reynolds number's of 17.3 and 24.7 $10^6/$ft. Using currents as high as 4 amps, the goal was to study the combined effect of heat and momentum addition. Measurements were taken of the plasma column speed using different arrangements of electric and magnetic fields. The plasma speed was able to be accelerated by 330 ft/s over the local flow, or slowed to 330 ft/s slower than the local flow. Utilizing a self-aligned focusing Schlieren (SAFS) system and static wall pressure measurements, the impact of the SWBLI was studied. When using a current of 4 amps, the wall static pressure was able to be reduced by 6\%, depending on the orientation of the electric field. Using the SAFS system, the interaction was observed to move in the upstream direction by $\sim$ 0.2 inches when the plasma was on. This change is apparent in the mean and unsteady measurements.

recent_works.title: Demonstration of Supersonic Autoignition of Ethylene in a Model Scramjet
recent_works.abstract: Hypersonic air-breathing propulsion systems represent a critical enabling technology for sustained high-speed flight, yet the short residence times inherent to supersonic combustion impose fundamental constraints on fuel-air mixing, ignition, and flame stabilization. This paper presents experimental results from the design and verification of a model scramjet and an initial investigation of the autoignition ethylene in a model scramjet at the University of Notre Dame Mach 4 Reflected Shock Tunnel (M4ST). A weighted optimization algorithm was used to generate the most favorable scramjet inlet geometry based on a single set of tunnel stagnation conditions (T5=1038K, Re'=4.47*10^6 1/m, h_05=0.85 MJ/kg) targeting low-temperature autoignition near the ramjet-to-scramjet transition regime. Self-aligned focusing schlieren (SAFS) imaging confirmed the intended supersonic inlet shock structure and verified that the combustor section maintained supersonic flow with and without active fuel injection and autoignition.
